question: How long must an authorised representative keep the technical paperwork for a general-purpose AI?
answer_A: The authorised representative must keep the technical documentation for **10 years after the general-purpose AI model has been placed on the market** [Art. 54(3)].
answer_B:
An authorised representative of a provider of a general-purpose AI model must keep a copy of the technical documentation specified in Annex XI at the disposal of the AI Office and national competent authorities for a period of 10 years after the general-purpose AI model has been placed on the market [Art. 54(3)(b)].

(Later amendments to the Act are not reflected in this text.)
answer_C:
An authorised representative must keep a copy of the technical documentation specified in Annex XI for a period of **10 years** after the general-purpose AI model has been placed on the market [Art. 54(3)(b)]. 

During this period, the documentation—as well as the contact details of the provider—must be kept at the disposal of the AI Office and national competent authorities [Art. 54(3)(b)].

question: Can a high-risk AI be sold or used before its conformity checks are finished?
answer_A:
Yes, under specific exceptional circumstances and subject to strict conditions, a high-risk AI system can be placed on the market or put into service before its conformity assessment procedures are completed [Art. 46(1)], [Art. 46(2)]:

* **Market surveillance authority authorisation:** By way of derogation from Article 43 and upon a duly justified request, a market surveillance authority may authorise the placing on the market or putting into service of a specific high-risk AI system within its Member State's territory for "exceptional reasons of public security or the protection of life and health of persons, environmental protection or the protection of key industrial and infrastructural assets" [Art. 46(1)]. 
  * This authorisation is granted "for a limited period while the necessary conformity assessment procedures are being carried out", and the completion of those procedures must be undertaken without undue delay [Art. 46(1)].

* **Urgent use by law-enforcement or civil protection authorities:** In a "duly justified situation of urgency for exceptional reasons of public security or in the case of specific, substantial and imminent threat to the life or physical safety of natural persons," law-enforcement or civil protection authorities may put a specific high-risk AI system into service without prior authorisation [Art. 46(2)].
  * Such authorisation must be requested "during or after the use without undue delay" [Art. 46(2)].
  * If the authorisation is refused, use must be stopped immediately and all results and outputs immediately discarded [Art. 46(2)].

Outside these derogations, placing on the market or putting into service generally requires undergoing the relevant conformity assessment procedures [Art. 23(1)(a)], [Art. 43(1)], [Art. 43(3)].
answer_B:
Under the provided excerpts, a high-risk AI system can be put into service without the prior authorisation under a derogation from conformity assessment only in specific urgent circumstances [Art. 46(2)]:

* **Urgent derogation for public safety:** Law-enforcement authorities or civil protection authorities may put a specific high-risk AI system into service without the authorisation in a "duly justified situation of urgency for exceptional reasons of public security or in the case of specific, substantial and imminent threat to the life or physical safety of natural persons" [Art. 46(2)].
* **Conditions:** 
  * Such authorisation must be "requested during or after the use without undue delay" [Art. 46(2)].
  * If the authorisation is refused, "the use of the high-risk AI system shall be stopped with immediate effect and all the results and outputs of such use shall be immediately discarded" [Art. 46(2)].

Outside of this derogation, systems covered by Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I are required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment with a view to being placed on the market or put into service [Art. 6(1)(b)]. (Note: The provided excerpts do not include the full text of Article 46(1) or the broader general conformity assessment requirements).
answer_C: No. A high-risk AI system cannot be placed on the market or put into service before the conformity assessment is completed: the provider must “ensure that the high-risk AI system undergoes the relevant conformity assessment procedure … prior to its being placed on the market or put into service” [Art. 16]. Importers must likewise verify, before placing the system on the market, that “the relevant conformity assessment procedure referred to in Article 43 has been carried out by the provider” [Art. 23(1)], and both the provider and the system must be registered in the EU database before placing on the market or putting into service [Art. 49(1)].

question: Under Article 60(4)(h), what do providers need to do when they team up with deployers for real-world testing?
answer_A: When providers or prospective providers organize real-world testing in cooperation with one or more deployers or prospective deployers, they must: inform those deployers of all aspects of the testing relevant to their decision to participate, and give them the relevant instructions for use of the AI system referred to in Article 13; and conclude an agreement with the deployer or prospective deployer specifying their roles and responsibilities to ensure compliance with the testing provisions under the Regulation and other applicable Union and national law [Art. 60(4)(h)].
answer_B:
Under Article 60(4)(h), when a provider or prospective provider organizes real-world testing in cooperation with one or more deployers or prospective deployers, they must ensure the following:

* Inform the deployers or prospective deployers of "all aspects of the testing that are relevant to their decision to participate" [Art. 60(4)(h)].
* Provide them with the "relevant instructions for use of the AI system referred to in Article 13" [Art. 60(4)(h)].
* Conclude an agreement with the deployer or prospective deployer "specifying their roles and responsibilities with a view to ensuring compliance with the provisions for testing in real world conditions under this Regulation and under other applicable Union and national law" [Art. 60(4)(h)].
answer_C:
Under Article 60(4)(h) of the EU AI Act, when a provider or prospective provider organises real-world testing in cooperation with one or more deployers or prospective deployers, they must ensure the following [Art. 60(4)(h)]:

* **Inform the deployers:** The deployer or prospective deployer must be "informed of all aspects of the testing that are relevant to their decision to participate" [Art. 60(4)(h)].
* **Provide instructions:** The provider must give them the "relevant instructions for use of the AI system referred to in Article 13" [Art. 60(4)(h)].
* **Conclude an agreement:** The provider (or prospective provider) and the deployer (or prospective deployer) must "conclude an agreement specifying their roles and responsibilities with a view to ensuring compliance with the provisions for testing in real world conditions under this Regulation and under other applicable Union and national law" [Art. 60(4)(h)].

question: If my company already has a monitoring plan under other EU laws, can we just add the AI Act requirements to it instead of making a new one?
answer_A: Yes, but only in the specific cases covered: for high-risk AI systems covered by Union harmonisation legislation listed in Section A of Annex I, providers “shall have a choice of integrating” the required elements into systems and plans already existing under that legislation, provided this achieves “an equivalent level of protection” [Art. 72(4)]. The same applies to Annex III point 5 high-risk AI systems placed on the market by financial institutions subject to Union financial-services-law internal governance requirements [Art. 72(4)]. The AI Act still requires the monitoring system/plan to meet the general requirements, including being proportionate and documented [Art. 72(1)] and based on a plan forming part of the technical documentation [Art. 72(3)]. This is not legal advice.
answer_B:
Yes, under specific conditions set out in the AI Act, your company may integrate the AI Act's post-market monitoring requirements into an existing plan rather than creating a separate one [Art. 72(4)].

Under Article 72(4), providers have the choice of integrating the necessary elements into existing systems and plans, provided that this "achieves an equivalent level of protection," in the following cases:
* **Union harmonisation legislation:** For high-risk AI systems covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Section A of Annex I where a post-market monitoring system and plan are already established under that legislation [Art. 72(4)].
* **Financial institutions:** For high-risk AI systems referred to in point 5 of Annex III placed on the market or put into service by financial institutions subject to requirements under Union financial services law regarding internal governance, arrangements, or processes [Art. 72(4)].

When integrating these requirements:
* You must integrate the necessary elements described in Article 72(1), (2), and (3) using the template established by the Commission [Art. 72(4)]. The Commission is to adopt an implementing act establishing this template and list of elements by 2 February 2026 [Art. 72(3)]. (Later amendments to the Act are not reflected in this text.)
* The integrated system must still be proportionate to the AI technologies and risks [Art. 72(1)], actively and systematically collect and analyze relevant performance data to evaluate continuous compliance with Chapter III, Section 2 [Art. 72(2)], and remain part of the technical documentation referred to in Annex IV [Art. 72(3)].

This explanation is based on the criteria in the Act and does not constitute legal advice.
answer_C:
Yes, under specific conditions, you have the choice to integrate the AI Act requirements into your existing system and plan rather than creating a completely separate one [Art. 72(4)].

According to the Act, this option is available under the following criteria:
* **Applicable systems:** It applies to high-risk AI systems covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Section A of Annex I (where a post-market monitoring system and plan are already established under that legislation), as well as high-risk AI systems referred to in point 5 of Annex III placed on the market or put into service by financial institutions subject to Union financial services law requirements regarding internal governance, arrangements, or processes [Art. 72(4)].
* **Integration requirements:** Providers may integrate, as appropriate, the necessary elements described in Article 72(1), (2), and (3) using the designated template into their existing systems and plans [Art. 72(4)].
* **Level of protection:** This integration is permitted "provided that it achieves an equivalent level of protection" [Art. 72(4)].
* **Template deadline:** The Commission is required to adopt an implementing act establishing the template and list of elements for the post-market monitoring plan by 2 February 2026 (later amendments to the Act are not reflected in this text) [Art. 72(3)].

This is not legal advice.

question: Can providers of high-risk AI systems check their own compliance without using an external organization?
answer_A:
Yes. For high-risk AI systems referred to in points 2 to 8 of Annex III, providers must use the conformity assessment procedure based on internal control, which “does not provide for the involvement of a notified body” [Art. 43(2)]. For high-risk AI systems listed in point 1 of Annex III, the provider may opt for internal control under Annex VI, unless specific exceptions apply (such as the absence of harmonised standards or their partial application) [Art. 43(1)].

The internal control procedure requires the provider itself to verify quality management system compliance, examine the technical documentation, and check that the design, development and post-market monitoring are consistent with that documentation [Annex VI]. This reflects the general rule that conformity assessment for high-risk AI systems (other than those related to products) is carried out by the provider under its own responsibility [Recital 125].
answer_B:
Yes, providers can perform conformity assessments internally without the involvement of a notified body under certain conditions [Art. 43(1)], [Art. 43(2)], [Art. 43(3)]:

* **Annex III, points 2 to 8 systems:** For high-risk AI systems referred to in points 2 to 8 of Annex III, providers are required to follow the conformity assessment procedure based on internal control (referred to in Annex VI), "which does not provide for the involvement of a notified body" [Art. 43(2)].
* **Annex III, point 1 systems:** Providers may opt for the internal control procedure under Annex VI if they have applied harmonised standards or, where applicable, common specifications to demonstrate compliance with the requirements in Section 2 [Art. 43(1)]. 
  * However, providers *must* follow the Annex VII procedure (involving a notified body) if harmonised standards do not exist and common specifications are unavailable, if the provider has not applied them (or applied them only in part), or if a standard was published with a restriction [Art. 43(1)].
* **Annex I, Section A systems:** For high-risk AI systems covered by Union harmonisation legislation listed in Section A of Annex I, if that legal act allows the manufacturer to opt out from a third-party conformity assessment, the manufacturer may only use that opt-out option if it has applied harmonised standards or common specifications covering all requirements set out in Section 2 of Chapter III [Art. 43(3)].
answer_C:
Yes, in many cases providers can check their own compliance without using an external organization (notified body), though it depends on the classification of the high-risk AI system and whether specific standards are met:

* **High-risk AI systems in points 2 to 8 of Annex III:** Providers must follow the conformity assessment procedure based on internal control set out in Annex VI, which "does not provide for the involvement of a notified body" [Art. 43(2)], [Recital 125]. Under this procedure, the provider itself verifies compliance regarding its quality management system, technical documentation, design and development process, and post-market monitoring [Annex VI, points 1–4].
* **High-risk AI systems in point 1 of Annex III:** Providers may opt for the internal control procedure under Annex VI (without a notified body) *only if* they have applied harmonised standards (Article 40) or, where applicable, common specifications (Article 41) to demonstrate compliance [Art. 43(1)]. If those standards or specifications do not exist, are not available, are not fully applied, or have restrictions, the provider must use an external notified body under Annex VII [Art. 43(1)].
* **Systems covered by Union harmonisation legislation in Section A of Annex I:** Providers must follow the relevant conformity assessment procedure required under those legal acts [Art. 43(3)]. If such a legal act allows a manufacturer to opt out of third-party conformity assessment when applying all relevant harmonised standards, the manufacturer may only use that option if it has also applied harmonised standards or common specifications covering all Chapter III, Section 2 requirements [Art. 43(3)].

question: Can the Commission bring in outside experts to help evaluate general-purpose AI models?
answer_A:
Yes. The Commission may decide to appoint independent experts to carry out evaluations on its behalf, including experts from the scientific panel established pursuant to Article 68 [Art. 92(2)]. 

Key conditions and details include:
* **Criteria:** Independent experts appointed to carry out evaluations must meet the criteria in Article 68(2) [Art. 92(2)], which require:
  * particular expertise, competence, and up-to-date scientific or technical expertise in the field of AI [Art. 68(2), Art. 68(2)(a)];
  * independence from any provider of AI systems or general-purpose AI models [Art. 68(2)(b)]; and
  * an ability to carry out activities diligently, accurately, and objectively [Art. 68(2)(c)].
* **Arrangements and selection:** The Commission is required to adopt implementing acts that set out the detailed arrangements and conditions for evaluations, including the detailed arrangements for involving independent experts and the procedure for selecting them [Art. 92(6)].
answer_B:
Yes, the Commission may decide to appoint independent experts to carry out evaluations of general-purpose AI models on its behalf, including experts from the scientific panel established pursuant to Article 68 [Art. 92(2)]. 

Key conditions include:
* **Eligibility criteria:** Independent experts appointed for this task must meet the criteria in Article 68(2), demonstrating:
  * particular expertise and competence as well as scientific or technical expertise in the field of AI [Art. 68(2)(a)],
  * independence from any provider of AI systems or general-purpose AI models [Art. 68(2)(b)], and
  * the ability to carry out activities diligently, accurately, and objectively [Art. 68(2)(c)].
* **Implementing acts:** The Commission must adopt implementing acts detailing the arrangements and conditions for evaluations, including the procedure for selecting independent experts and the detailed arrangements for their involvement [Art. 92(6)].
answer_C: Yes. The Commission may appoint independent experts to carry out evaluations of general-purpose AI models on its behalf, including experts from the scientific panel established under Article 68 [Art. 92(2)]. These independent experts must meet the criteria set out in Article 68(2): particular expertise and competence in AI, independence from any provider of AI systems or general-purpose AI models, and an ability to carry out activities diligently, accurately and objectively [Art. 68(2)]. The Commission is to adopt implementing acts setting out the detailed arrangements and conditions for such evaluations, including the arrangements for involving and selecting independent experts [Art. 92(6)].

question: What does the Commission have to do when a new European technical standard is officially published?
answer_A:
When a reference to a harmonised standard is published in the Official Journal of the European Union, the Commission must repeal the implementing acts establishing common specifications (referred to in Article 41(1)), or parts thereof, which cover [Art. 41(4)]:

* the same requirements set out in Section 2 of Chapter III; or
* as applicable, the same obligations set out in Sections 2 and 3 of Chapter V [Art. 41(4)].

Additionally, prior to publication, when a harmonised standard is adopted by a European standardisation organisation and proposed for the publication of its reference in the Official Journal, the Commission must assess it in accordance with Regulation (EU) No 1025/2012 [Art. 41(4)].
answer_B: When a reference to a harmonised standard is published in the Official Journal of the European Union, the Commission shall repeal the implementing acts (common specifications) adopted under Article 41(1), or the parts thereof, that cover the same requirements set out in Section 2 of Chapter III or, as applicable, the same obligations set out in Sections 2 and 3 of Chapter V [Art. 41(4)].
answer_C:
When a reference to a harmonised standard adopted by a European standardisation organisation is published in the Official Journal of the European Union, the Commission must:

* Repeal the implementing acts establishing common specifications (referred to in Article 41(1)), or parts thereof, that cover the same requirements set out in Chapter III, Section 2, or, as applicable, the same obligations set out in Chapter V, Sections 2 and 3 [Art. 41(4)].

Prior to this publication, when the standard is proposed to the Commission, the Commission must assess it in accordance with Regulation (EU) No 1025/2012 [Art. 41(4)].

question: Do I need to register my high-risk AI system in an EU database before I start selling or using it?
answer_A: Yes. Before placing on the market or putting into service a high-risk AI system listed in Annex III (except point 2 of Annex III), the provider or authorised representative must register themselves and the system in the EU database [Art. 49(1)]. Before putting into service or using such a system, deployers that are public authorities, Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies (or persons acting on their behalf) must also register themselves, select the system and register its use [Art. 49(3)], and they must comply with these registration obligations and shall not use the system if it is not registered [Art. 26(8)]. Additionally, if a provider concludes that an Annex III system is not high-risk under Article 6(3), they must still register themselves and that system before placing it on the market or putting it into service [Art. 49(2)].
answer_B:
Whether you must register your AI system in the EU database before placing it on the market ("selling") or using it depends on your role and the classification of the system:

* **If you are a provider (or authorised representative):**
  * Before placing on the market or putting into service a high-risk AI system listed in Annex III, you must register yourself and your system in the EU database referred to in Article 71 [Art. 49(1)]. 
  * *Exception:* Systems referred to in point 2 of Annex III are excluded from this registration obligation [Art. 49(1)].
  * *Note on derogations:* Even if you conclude that an AI system referred to in Annex III is not high-risk according to Article 6(3), you must still register yourself and that system in the EU database prior to placing it on the market or putting it into service [Art. 49(2)], [Art. 6(4)].

* **If you are a deployer (user):**
  * You must register in the EU database before putting into service or using a high-risk AI system listed in Annex III only if you are a public authority, Union institution, body, office or agency, or a person acting on their behalf [Art. 49(3)], [Art. 26(8)]. In that case, you must register yourself, select the system, and register its use [Art. 49(3)].
  * *Exception:* High-risk AI systems listed in point 2 of Annex III are excluded from this obligation [Art. 49(3)].
  * If you are such a public deployer and find that the system has not been registered in the database, you must not use the system and must inform the provider or distributor [Art. 26(8)].
  * The provided provisions do not establish registration requirements for private deployers [Art. 49(3)], [Art. 26(8)].

This is not legal advice.
answer_C:
Whether you must register your AI system in the EU database before selling (placing on the market) or using it depends on your role and the specific type of AI system:

* **If you are a provider:**
  * Before placing on the market or putting into service a high-risk AI system listed in Annex III, you (or your authorized representative) must register yourself and your system in the EU database referred to in Article 71 [Art. 49(1)].
  * *Exception:* This registration requirement does not apply to high-risk AI systems referred to in point 2 of Annex III [Art. 49(1)].
  * *Systems assessed as not high-risk:* If your system is referred to in Annex III but you have concluded it is not high-risk pursuant to Article 6(3), you must document that assessment and still register yourself and that system in the EU database before placing it on the market or putting it into service [Art. 49(2)], [Art. 6(4)].

* **If you are a deployer (user):**
  * You are only required to register if you are a public authority, Union institution, body, office or agency, or a person acting on their behalf [Art. 49(3)], [Art. 26(8)]. 
  * If you fall into that category, before putting into service or using a high-risk AI system listed in Annex III (except those listed in point 2 of Annex III), you must register yourself, select the system, and register its use in the EU database [Art. 49(3)]. 
  * If such a deployer finds the system has not been registered in the database, they must not use it and must inform the provider or distributor [Art. 26(8)].

This is not legal advice.

question: Who can cancel a delegation of power, and does it affect rules that are already in place?
answer_A:
Under the EU Artificial Intelligence Act, the delegation of power may be revoked at any time by either:
* the **European Parliament**, or 
* the **Council** [Art. 97(3)].

A decision of revocation puts an end to the delegation of power specified in that decision, taking effect the day following its publication in the *Official Journal of the European Union* or at a later date specified therein [Art. 97(3)]. 

It **does not** affect rules that are already in place: the revocation "shall not affect the validity of any delegated acts already in force" [Art. 97(3)].
answer_B:
The delegation of power may be revoked at any time by the European Parliament or by the Council [Art. 97(3)]. 

A decision of revocation puts an end to the delegation of power specified in that decision, but it **does not affect the validity of any delegated acts already in force** [Art. 97(3)]. 

The revocation takes effect the day following its publication in the *Official Journal of the European Union* or at a later date specified in the decision [Art. 97(3)].
answer_C: The European Parliament or the Council may revoke the delegation of power at any time [Art. 97(3)]. Such a revocation shall not affect the validity of any delegated acts already in force [Art. 97(3)].

question: What language do AI conformity certificates need to be written in?
answer_A:
Certificates issued by notified bodies in accordance with Annex VII must be drawn up in a language that can be easily understood by the relevant authorities in the Member State in which the notified body is established [Art. 44(1)]. 

*(Note: In contrast, the EU declaration of conformity drawn up by the provider must be translated into a language that can be easily understood by the national competent authorities of the Member States in which the high-risk AI system is placed on the market or made available [Art. 47(2)].)*
answer_B: According to the EU AI Act, certificates issued by notified bodies must be drawn up in a language which can be easily understood by the relevant authorities in the Member State in which the notified body is established [Art. 44(1)].
answer_C: Certificates issued by notified bodies in accordance with Annex VII must be drawn up in a language that can be easily understood by the relevant authorities in the Member State in which the notified body is established [Art. 44(1)].

question: What will the AI Office do to help companies understand and follow the new AI rules?
answer_A:
The AI Office will help companies understand and follow the rules by:

*   Providing standardised templates for areas covered by the Regulation, developing and maintaining a single information platform providing easy-to-use information for all operators, organising communication campaigns to raise awareness about obligations, and evaluating and promoting best practices in public procurement procedures in relation to AI systems [Art. 62(3)].
*   Encouraging and facilitating the drawing up of codes of practice at Union level to facilitate the effective implementation of obligations regarding the detection and labelling of artificially generated or manipulated content [Art. 50(7)].
*   Encouraging and facilitating the review and adaptation of codes of practice, and assisting in the assessment of available standards [Art. 56(8)].

More generally, the Commission shall develop Union expertise and capabilities in the field of AI through the AI Office [Art. 64(1)].
answer_B:
To help operators understand and comply with the Regulation, the AI Office is tasked with the following actions:

* **Information and awareness:**
  * Develop and maintain a single information platform that provides "easy to use information in relation to this Regulation for all operators across the Union" [Art. 62(3)(b)].
  * Organise appropriate communication campaigns to raise awareness concerning the obligations arising from the Regulation [Art. 62(3)(c)].

* **Standardised tools and best practices:**
  * Provide standardised templates for areas covered by the Regulation, as requested by the European Artificial Intelligence Board [Art. 62(3)(a)].
  * Evaluate and promote the convergence of best practices in public procurement procedures concerning AI systems [Art. 62(3)(d)].

* **Codes of practice and standards:**
  * Encourage and facilitate the drawing up of Union-level codes of practice to support the effective implementation of obligations regarding the detection and labelling of artificially generated or manipulated content [Art. 50(7)].
  * Encourage and facilitate the review and adaptation of codes of practice (particularly considering emerging standards) and assist in assessing available standards [Art. 56(8)].
answer_C:
Based on the provided excerpts, the AI Office will undertake several actions to help companies and operators understand and follow the rules:

* **Provide standardized templates:** It will provide standardized templates for areas covered by the Regulation, as specified by the European Artificial Intelligence Board in its request [Art. 62(3)(a)].
* **Maintain an information platform:** It will develop and maintain a single information platform offering "easy to use information in relation to this Regulation for all operators across the Union" [Art. 62(3)(b)].
* **Raise awareness:** It will organize appropriate communication campaigns to raise awareness concerning the obligations arising from the Regulation [Art. 62(3)(c)].
* **Promote best practices in procurement:** It will evaluate and promote the convergence of best practices in public procurement procedures regarding AI systems [Art. 62(3)(d)].
* **Facilitate codes of practice:** 
  * It will encourage and facilitate the drawing up of Union-level codes of practice to support the effective implementation of obligations on detecting and labelling artificially generated or manipulated content [Art. 50(7)].
  * It should encourage and facilitate the drawing up, review, and adaptation of codes of practice covering obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models and those presenting systemic risks, inviting providers to participate and collaborating with authorities, experts, and stakeholders [Recital 116].

question: How are the members of the AI scientific panel chosen, and what qualifications do they need?
answer_A: Members of the scientific panel are selected by the Commission on the basis of up-to-date scientific or technical expertise in the field of AI necessary for the tasks set out in Article 68(3) [Art. 68(2)]. To be selected, experts must be able to demonstrate that they meet all of the following conditions: (a) having particular expertise and competence and scientific or technical expertise in the field of AI; (b) independence from any provider of AI systems or general-purpose AI models; and (c) an ability to carry out activities diligently, accurately and objectively [Art. 68(2)]. The Commission, in consultation with the Board, determines the number of experts on the panel and ensures fair gender and geographical representation [Art. 68(2)]. Once appointed, experts must perform their tasks with impartiality and objectivity, ensure confidentiality, and neither seek nor take instructions from anyone [Art. 68(4)].
answer_B:
Members of the scientific panel are selected by the Commission [Art. 68(2)]. 

**Selection process and composition:**
* The Commission establishes the scientific panel by means of an implementing act adopted in accordance with the examination procedure [Art. 68(1)].
* The Commission determines the number of experts on the panel in consultation with the Board, in accordance with required needs [Art. 68(2)].
* The Commission must ensure "fair gender and geographical representation" [Art. 68(2)].

**Qualifications and conditions:**
Experts are selected on the basis of "up-to-date scientific or technical expertise in the field of AI necessary for the tasks" [Art. 68(2)], and must be able to demonstrate meeting all of the following conditions:
* Having "particular expertise and competence and scientific or technical expertise in the field of AI" [Art. 68(2)(a)];
* "Independence from any provider of AI systems or general-purpose AI models" [Art. 68(2)(b)];
* "An ability to carry out activities diligently, accurately and objectively" [Art. 68(2)(c)].
answer_C:
Under the EU AI Act, members of the scientific panel are chosen and qualified according to the following rules:

**Selection Process**
* The experts are selected by the Commission on the basis of up-to-date scientific or technical expertise in the field of AI necessary for their tasks [Art. 68(2)].
* The Commission, in consultation with the European Artificial Intelligence Board, determines the number of experts on the panel according to required needs and must ensure fair gender and geographical representation [Art. 68(2)].
* The Commission makes provisions on the establishment of the panel by means of an implementing act adopted in accordance with the examination procedure [Art. 68(1)].

**Required Qualifications and Conditions**
The selected experts must be able to demonstrate that they meet all of the following conditions:
* Having particular expertise and competence and scientific or technical expertise in the field of AI [Art. 68(2)];
* Independence from any provider of AI systems or general-purpose AI models [Art. 68(2)];
* An ability to carry out activities diligently, accurately, and objectively [Art. 68(2)].

Additionally, experts must perform their tasks with impartiality and objectivity, ensure the confidentiality of information and data obtained, neither seek nor take instructions from anyone, and draw up a declaration of interests that is made publicly available [Art. 68(4)].

question: What must a company do if their high-risk AI doesn't follow the common specifications?
answer_A:
If a provider's high-risk AI system does not comply with the established common specifications, the company must:

* **Duly justify equivalent technical solutions:** The provider must "duly justify that they have adopted technical solutions that meet the requirements referred to in Section 2 of this Chapter or, as applicable, comply with the obligations set out in Sections 2 and 3 of Chapter V to a level at least equivalent thereto" [Art. 41(5)].
* **Follow a specific conformity assessment procedure:** 
  * For high-risk AI systems listed in point 1 of Annex III, if common specifications exist but the provider has not applied them (or has not applied harmonised standards), the provider cannot rely on internal control and "shall follow the conformity assessment procedure set out in Annex VII" involving a notified body [Art. 43(1)].
  * For systems covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Section A of Annex I where the legislation allows opting out of third-party conformity assessment upon applying all standards, the manufacturer cannot use that opt-out option unless it has applied the harmonised standards or common specifications covering all Section 2 requirements [Art. 43(3)].

This is not legal advice.
answer_B:
If a high-risk AI system does not comply with the applicable common specifications, the provider must:

* **Duly justify equivalent technical solutions:** The provider must "duly justify that they have adopted technical solutions that meet the requirements referred to in Section 2 of this Chapter... to a level at least equivalent thereto" [Art. 41(5)].
* **Follow a specific conformity assessment procedure (for Annex III, point 1 systems):** In demonstrating compliance with the requirements set out in Section 2 for high-risk AI systems listed in point 1 of Annex III, where common specifications exist but the provider has not applied them, the provider cannot rely on internal control and "shall follow the conformity assessment procedure set out in Annex VII" (involving the assessment of the quality management system and technical documentation with a notified body) [Art. 43(1)].

This is not legal advice.
answer_C:
If a company's high-risk AI system does not comply with the common specifications, it must duly justify that it has adopted technical solutions meeting the requirements of Section 2 of Chapter III (or, as applicable, the obligations in Sections 2 and 3 of Chapter V) to a level at least equivalent thereto [Art. 41(5)].

Additionally, where common specifications exist but the provider has not applied them, the provider shall follow the conformity assessment procedure set out in Annex VII [Art. 43(1)].

question: What can the Commission do after receiving a qualified alert?
answer_A:
Upon receiving a qualified alert, the Commission can take the following actions:

* **Exercise supervisory and enforcement powers:** The Commission, acting through the AI Office and after having informed the Board, may exercise the powers laid down in Section 5 (Chapter IX) for the purpose of assessing the matter [Art. 90(2)]. The AI Office must inform the Board of any measure taken according to Articles 91 to 94 [Art. 90(2)].
* **Designate a model as presenting systemic risks:** Following a qualified alert from the scientific panel pursuant to Article 90(1), point (a), the Commission may designate a general-purpose AI model as presenting systemic risks on the basis of the criteria set out in Annex XIII [Art. 52(4)].
* **Receive Board opinions:** The Commission may receive opinions from the Board on the qualified alerts regarding general-purpose AI models [Art. 66(n)].
answer_B:
Upon receiving a qualified alert, the Commission may exercise the powers laid down in Section 5 (supervision, investigation, enforcement and monitoring in respect of providers of general-purpose AI models) for the purpose of assessing the matter. This is done through the AI Office and after having informed the Board; the AI Office must then inform the Board of any measure taken according to Articles 91 to 94 [Art. 90(2)].

In addition, the Commission may designate the general-purpose AI model as presenting systemic risks, following a qualified alert from the scientific panel under Article 90(1), point (a), on the basis of the criteria set out in Annex XIII [Art. 52(4)].
answer_C:
Upon receiving a qualified alert regarding a general-purpose AI model, the Commission may:

* **Exercise investigatory and enforcement powers:** Through the AI Office and after having informed the Board, the Commission "may exercise the powers laid down in this Section for the purpose of assessing the matter" [Art. 90(2)]. The AI Office must inform the Board of any measure taken according to Articles 91 to 94 [Art. 90(2)].
* **Designate the model as presenting systemic risks:** Following a qualified alert from the scientific panel pursuant to Article 90(1), point (a), the Commission may designate the general-purpose AI model as presenting systemic risks on the basis of the criteria set out in Annex XIII [Art. 52(4)].

Additionally, in connection with these alerts, the Commission may receive opinions from the Board [Art. 66(n)].

question: How will the rules for running evaluations and picking outside experts be decided?
answer_A:
The rules for conducting evaluations and selecting outside experts are decided as follows:

* **Adoption of implementing acts:** The Commission must adopt implementing acts setting out the detailed arrangements and conditions for the evaluations, including the procedure for selecting independent experts and the arrangements for involving them [Art. 92(6)]. These implementing acts must be adopted in accordance with the examination procedure referred to in Article 98(2) [Art. 92(6)].
* **Appointment of independent experts:** The Commission may appoint independent experts to carry out evaluations on its behalf, including members from the scientific panel established under Article 68 [Art. 92(2)].
* **Selection criteria for experts:** Independent experts appointed for evaluations must meet the criteria in Article 68(2) [Art. 92(2)]:
  * have particular expertise and competence, as well as up-to-date scientific or technical expertise in the field of AI [Art. 68(2)], [Art. 68(2)(a)];
  * be independent from any provider of AI systems or general-purpose AI models [Art. 68(2)(b)];
  * demonstrate an ability to carry out activities diligently, accurately, and objectively [Art. 68(2)(c)].
* **Panel composition requirements:** When selecting panel experts, the Commission—in consultation with the European Artificial Intelligence Board—determines the number of experts needed and must ensure fair gender and geographical representation [Art. 68(2)].
answer_B:
The Commission will adopt implementing acts setting out the detailed arrangements and conditions for the evaluations, including the arrangements for involving independent experts and the procedure for their selection, under the examination procedure referred to in Article 98(2) [Art. 92(6)].

For outside experts, the Commission may appoint independent experts to carry out evaluations on its behalf, including from the scientific panel, and they must meet the criteria in Article 68(2) [Art. 92(2)]. Those criteria require up-to-date scientific or technical expertise in AI, particular expertise and competence in AI, independence from any provider of AI systems or general-purpose AI models, and an ability to carry out activities diligently, accurately and objectively [Art. 68(2)]. The experts must perform their tasks with impartiality and objectivity, ensure confidentiality, neither seek nor take instructions from anyone, and draw up a publicly available declaration of interests [Art. 68(4)].
answer_C:
Under the EU Artificial Intelligence Act, the rules for running evaluations and selecting outside experts are decided as follows:

* **Implementing Acts by the Commission:** The Commission must adopt implementing acts that set out the detailed arrangements and conditions for evaluations, including the procedure for selecting independent experts and the detailed arrangements for involving them [Art. 92(6)]. These acts are adopted in accordance with the examination procedure referred to in Article 98(2) [Art. 92(6)].
* **Appointment and Sources of Experts:** The Commission may decide to appoint independent experts to carry out evaluations on its behalf, which can include experts from the scientific panel established under Article 68 [Art. 92(2)].
* **Criteria for Independent Experts:** Any independent experts appointed for this task must satisfy the criteria set out in Article 68(2) [Art. 92(2)]:
  * Possess particular expertise, competence, and up-to-date scientific or technical expertise in the field of AI [Art. 68(2), Art. 68(2)(a)];
  * Demonstrate independence from any provider of AI systems or general-purpose AI models [Art. 68(2)(b)];
  * Demonstrate an ability to carry out activities diligently, accurately, and objectively [Art. 68(2)(c)].

question: When does a company that makes a product count as the provider of a high-risk AI safety component inside it?
answer_A:
A product manufacturer is considered to be the provider of a high-risk AI system that is a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Section A of Annex I, and is subject to the obligations under Article 16, under either of the following circumstances [Art. 25(3)]:

* the high-risk AI system is placed on the market together with the product under the name or trademark of the product manufacturer [Art. 25(3)(a)]; or
* the high-risk AI system is put into service under the name or trademark of the product manufacturer after the product has been placed on the market [Art. 25(3)(b)].

Additionally, where such a high-risk AI safety component is not placed on the market or put into service independently from the product, the product manufacturer should comply with provider obligations and ensure that the embedded AI system complies with the requirements of the Regulation [Recital 87].
answer_B:
A product manufacturer is considered the provider of a high-risk AI safety component inside its product when that AI system meets the high-risk conditions in [Art. 6(1)]—i.e., it is intended as a safety component of a product covered by Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and that product is required to undergo third-party conformity assessment (“safety component” is defined in [Art. 3(14)])—and either:

- the high-risk AI system is placed on the market together with the product under the name or trademark of the product manufacturer; or
- the high-risk AI system is put into service under the name or trademark of the product manufacturer after the product has been placed on the market [Art. 25(3)].
answer_C:
Under the AI Act, in the case of high-risk AI systems that are safety components of products covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Section A of Annex I, the product manufacturer is considered to be the provider of the high-risk AI system (and subject to the obligations under Article 16) under either of the following circumstances [Art. 25(3)]:

* The high-risk AI system is placed on the market together with the product under the name or trademark of the product manufacturer [Art. 25(3)(a)]; or
* The high-risk AI system is put into service under the name or trademark of the product manufacturer after the product has been placed on the market [Art. 25(3)(b)].

For context, a safety component is defined as a component of a product or of an AI system that fulfills a safety function for that product or AI system, or whose failure or malfunctioning endangers the health and safety of persons or property [Art. 3(14)]. Recital 87 also notes that where such a high-risk AI safety component is not placed on the market or put into service independently from the product, the product manufacturer should comply with provider obligations and ensure the embedded AI system complies with the Regulation's requirements [Recital 87].

question: How and where do I need to put the CE mark on a high-risk AI product?
answer_A:
Under the EU Artificial Intelligence Act, the criteria for how and where to affix the CE marking to a high-risk AI system are as follows:

* **Physical placement:** The CE marking must be affixed "visibly, legibly and indelibly for high-risk AI systems" [Art. 48(3)]. Where this is "not possible or not warranted on account of the nature of the high-risk AI system", it must be affixed to the packaging or to the accompanying documentation, as appropriate [Art. 48(3)], [Art. 16(h)].
* **Digitally provided systems:** For high-risk AI systems provided digitally, "a digital CE marking shall be used, only if it can easily be accessed via the interface from which that system is accessed or via an easily accessible machine-readable code or other electronic means" [Art. 48(2)].
* **General principles:** The CE marking is subject to the general principles set out in Article 30 of Regulation (EC) No 765/2008 [Art. 48(1)].
* **Notified body identification number:** Where applicable, the CE marking must be followed by the identification number of the notified body responsible for the conformity assessment procedures [Art. 48(4)]. This number must be affixed by the notified body itself or, under its instructions, by the provider or the provider’s authorised representative, and it must also appear in relevant promotional material [Art. 48(4)].
* **Other Union legislation:** If the high-risk AI system is subject to other Union law providing for the CE marking, the marking indicates that the system also fulfills the requirements of that other law [Art. 48(5)].

This is not legal advice.
answer_B:
Under the EU AI Act, the rules for affixing the CE marking on a high-risk AI system are as follows:

* **General Rule and Placement:** The provider must affix the CE marking visibly, legibly, and indelibly to the high-risk AI system itself [Art. 16(h)], [Art. 48(3)]. 
* **Alternative Placement:** Where affixing it directly to the system is "not possible or not warranted on account of the nature of the high-risk AI system," it must be affixed to the packaging or to the accompanying documentation, as appropriate [Art. 16(h)], [Art. 48(3)].
* **Digitally Provided Systems:** For systems provided digitally, a digital CE marking must be used "only if it can easily be accessed via the interface from which that system is accessed or via an easily accessible machine-readable code or other electronic means" [Art. 48(2)].
* **General Principles:** The CE marking is subject to the general principles set out in Article 30 of Regulation (EC) No 765/2008 [Art. 48(1)].
* **Notified Body Number:** Where applicable, the CE marking must be followed by the identification number of the notified body responsible for the conformity assessment procedures, affixed either by the body itself or by the provider (or their authorised representative) under the body's instructions [Art. 48(4)].
* **Other Union Law:** If the system is also subject to other Union law requiring CE marking, the CE marking indicates that the system also fulfills the requirements of that other law [Art. 48(5)].

This is not legal advice.
answer_C:
According to the EU AI Act, you must affix the CE marking **visibly, legibly and indelibly** on the high-risk AI system itself [Art. 48(3)]. If that is not possible or not warranted due to the nature of the system, you must affix it to the **packaging or accompanying documentation** instead [Art. 48(3)].

For high-risk AI systems **provided digitally**, you must use a **digital CE marking** that can easily be accessed via the interface from which the system is accessed, or via an easily accessible machine-readable code or other electronic means [Art. 48(2)].

Where applicable, the CE marking must be followed by the **identification number of the notified body** responsible for the conformity assessment; this number is affixed by the body itself or under its instructions, and must also appear in any promotional material mentioning CE conformity [Art. 48(4)].

As a provider, you are obligated to affix the CE marking to the system (or its packaging/documentation where not possible) to indicate conformity [Art. 16(h)]. The CE marking indicates that the system conforms with the requirements of Chapter III, Section 2 and other applicable Union harmonisation legislation [Art. 3(24)].

question: Are there any situations where the right to an explanation for an AI decision doesn't apply?
answer_A: Yes. The right to an explanation does not apply where exceptions or restrictions to that obligation follow from Union or national law in compliance with Union law [Art. 86(2)]. It also applies only to the extent that the right is not already otherwise provided for under Union law [Art. 86(3)]. These limits are reflected in the recitals as well [Recital 171].
answer_B:
Yes, under Article 86, the right to obtain an explanation of individual decision-making does not apply in several situations:

* **Annex III, point 2 systems:** High-risk AI systems listed under point 2 of Annex III are expressly excluded from the right to explanation [Art. 86(1)].
* **Exceptions or restrictions in Union or national law:** It does not apply to the use of AI systems where exceptions from, or restrictions to, this obligation follow from Union or national law in compliance with Union law [Art. 86(2)], [Recital 171].
* **Already covered by Union law:** The right applies only to the extent that it is not otherwise provided for under Union law [Art. 86(3)], [Recital 171].
* **Decisions outside the impact threshold:** The right only arises when a decision produces "legal effects or similarly significantly affects" a person in a way they consider to have an adverse impact on their "health, safety or fundamental rights" [Art. 86(1)], [Recital 171].
* **Systems not qualifying as Annex III high-risk:** The right applies to decisions based on outputs of high-risk AI systems listed in Annex III [Art. 86(1)]; it does not apply if an AI system is not considered high-risk, such as through the derogation under Article 6(3) where a system does not pose a significant risk of harm [Art. 6(3)].
* **General scope exclusions:** The Regulation itself does not apply to areas outside the scope of Union law, or to AI systems used exclusively for military, defence, or national security purposes [Art. 2(3)].
answer_C:
Yes, under the EU AI Act, the right to an explanation under Article 86 does not apply in several situations:

* **High-risk systems listed under point 2 of Annex III:** High-risk AI systems listed in Annex III are covered, "with the exception of systems listed under point 2 thereof" [Art. 86(1)].
* **Exceptions or restrictions under law:** The right does not apply to the use of AI systems for which "exceptions from, or restrictions to, the obligation... follow from Union or national law in compliance with Union law" [Art. 86(2)], [Recital 171].
* **Right already provided under Union law:** Article 86 applies "only to the extent that the right referred to in paragraph 1 is not otherwise provided for under Union law" [Art. 86(3)], [Recital 171].
* **Threshold criteria not met:** The right is conditional and does not arise if the decision taken on the basis of the AI system's output does not produce "legal effects or similarly significantly affects that person in a way that they consider to have an adverse impact on their health, safety or fundamental rights" [Art. 86(1)].
* **General scope exclusions of the Regulation:** The Act itself does not apply to areas outside the scope of Union law, activities concerning national security, or AI systems placed on the market, put into service, or used exclusively for military, defence, or national security purposes [Art. 2(3)].

question: What needs to be considered when making sure a high-risk AI system meets the rules in Article 8(1)?
answer_A:
When ensuring that a high-risk AI system complies with the requirements of Chapter III, Section 2, the following must be taken into account:

* The system's **intended purpose** [Art. 8(1)];
* The **generally acknowledged state of the art** on AI and AI-related technologies [Art. 8(1)]; and
* The **risk management system** referred to in Article 9 [Art. 8(1)].
answer_B: When ensuring a high-risk AI system complies with the requirements in Article 8(1), the following must be taken into account: the system's **intended purpose**, the **generally acknowledged state of the art on AI and AI-related technologies**, and the **risk management system referred to in Article 9** [Art. 8(1)].

question: What does a company have to do before launching an AI system they believe isn't high-risk?
answer_A: A company that considers its AI system not high-risk must, before placing it on the market or putting it into service: (1) document its assessment that the system is not high-risk [Art. 6(4)]; and (2) register itself and the system in the EU database referred to in Article 71 [Art. 49(2)], [Art. 6(4)]. Upon request of national competent authorities, the provider must also provide the documentation of that assessment [Art. 6(4)].
answer_B:
Before placing on the market or putting into service an AI system referred to in Annex III that the provider considers or has concluded is not high-risk (according to Article 6(3)), the provider must:

* **Document the assessment:** The provider must document its assessment before the system is placed on the market or put into service [Art. 6(4)].
* **Register in the EU database:** The provider or, where applicable, its authorised representative must register themselves and the system in the EU database referred to in Article 71 prior to placing it on the market or putting it into service [Art. 6(4)], [Art. 49(2)].

Additionally, the provider must provide the documentation of the assessment upon request of national competent authorities [Art. 6(4)].
answer_C:
If a provider considers that an AI system referred to in Annex III is not high-risk, before placing that system on the market or putting it into service, it must:

* **Document its assessment:** The provider must document its assessment concluding that the system is not high-risk before the system is placed on the market or put into service [Art. 6(4)]. The provider must also provide this documentation upon request to national competent authorities [Art. 6(4)].
* **Register in the EU database:** The provider or, where applicable, its authorised representative must register themselves and the system in the EU database referred to in Article 71 before placing the system on the market or putting it into service [Art. 6(4)], [Art. 49(2)].

question: If a regulator objects to real-world AI testing or makes a decision about it, what information do they have to give the provider?
answer_A:
When a market surveillance authority takes a decision under Article 76(3) or issues an objection under Article 60(4), point (b), the decision or objection must indicate:

* the grounds for the decision or objection [Art. 76(4)]; and
* how the provider or prospective provider can challenge the decision or objection [Art. 76(4)].

For context, the decisions covered by this requirement include decisions to suspend or terminate the testing in real world conditions, or to require the modification of any aspect of the testing [Art. 76(3)].
answer_C: The regulator must indicate **the grounds** for the decision or objection and **how the provider or prospective provider can challenge** it [Art. 76(4)].

question: Who can fine EU agencies if they break the AI rules, and what factors determine the amount?
answer_A:
The **European Data Protection Supervisor** may impose administrative fines on Union institutions, bodies, offices and agencies falling within the scope of the Regulation [Art. 100(1)].

When deciding whether to impose a fine and its amount, it must consider all relevant circumstances and give due regard to: (a) the nature, gravity and duration of the infringement and its consequences, the purpose of the AI system, the number of affected persons and the level of damage; (b) the degree of responsibility, taking into account technical and organisational measures; (c) any action taken to mitigate damage to affected persons; (d) the degree of cooperation with the European Data Protection Supervisor to remedy the infringement and mitigate adverse effects, including compliance with previously ordered measures; (e) any similar previous infringements; (f) how the infringement became known, in particular whether and to what extent the institution notified it; and (g) the annual budget of the institution, body, office or agency [Art. 100(1)].

The maximum fines are EUR 1 500 000 for non-compliance with the Article 5 prohibitions [Art. 100(2)] and EUR 750 000 for other non-compliance [Art. 100(3)].

question: After finishing a fundamental rights assessment for a high-risk AI system, who do I have to report the results to?
answer_A:
Once the assessment has been performed, you must notify the **market surveillance authority** of its results [Art. 27(3)].

Key conditions and related reporting obligations include:
* **Submission format:** The notification must include the filled-out template developed by the AI Office (referred to in Article 27(5)) [Art. 27(3)].
* **Exception:** Deployers may be exempt from this obligation to notify in the case referred to in Article 46(1) [Art. 27(3)].
* **Registration submission:** Deployers required to register high-risk AI systems pursuant to Article 49(3) must also submit a summary of the findings of the fundamental rights impact assessment as part of the registration information [Annex VIII, Section C, points 1–5].
* **Access upon request:** Relevant national public authorities or bodies supervising or enforcing fundamental rights obligations have the power to request and access documentation created or maintained under the Regulation where necessary to fulfill their mandates [Art. 77(1)].

This information is for guidance based on the Regulation and does not constitute legal advice.
answer_B:
Once you have performed the fundamental rights impact assessment, you must report the results to the following entities:

* **The Market Surveillance Authority:** The deployer must notify the market surveillance authority of the results, submitting the filled-out template developed by the AI Office as part of the notification [Art. 27(3)], [Art. 27(5)]. *(Exception: in the case referred to in Article 46(1), deployers may be exempt from this obligation to notify [Art. 27(3)].)*
* **Registration in the EU Database:** Deployers required to register their high-risk AI system pursuant to Article 49(3) must submit a "summary of the findings of the fundamental rights impact assessment" as part of the registration information [Annex VIII, Section C, points 1–5].
* **Fundamental Rights Authorities (upon request):** National public authorities or bodies supervising or enforcing fundamental rights obligations have the power to request and access any documentation created or maintained under the Regulation when necessary to fulfill their mandates [Art. 77(1)].

This information is based on the statutory criteria provided and does not constitute legal advice.
answer_C: You must notify the **market surveillance authority** of the results, submitting the filled-out template as part of the notification [Art. 27(3)]. In the case referred to in Article 46(1), you may be exempt from that obligation to notify [Art. 27(3)].

question: How do notified bodies adapt their processes for different AI companies?
answer_A:
Notified bodies adapt their procedures by taking due account of the **size of the provider, the sector in which it operates, its structure, and the degree of complexity of the AI system concerned** [Art. 31(8)].

When performing their activities, they must also **avoid unnecessary burdens** for providers and take due account of these same factors—particularly with a view to **minimising administrative burdens and compliance costs for micro- and small enterprises**—while still respecting the degree of rigour and level of protection required for compliance with the Regulation [Art. 34(2)].
answer_B:
Under the EU AI Act, notified bodies adapt their processes by:

* **Implementing adaptive procedures:** Notified bodies must establish procedures for carrying out their activities that take due account of the size of a provider, the sector in which it operates, its structure, and the degree of complexity of the AI system concerned [Art. 31(8)].
* **Avoiding unnecessary burdens and minimising costs:** When performing their activities, notified bodies must avoid unnecessary burdens for providers and take due account of the provider's size, sector, structure, and the complexity of the high-risk AI system [Art. 34(2)]. This must be done "in particular in view of minimising administrative burdens and compliance costs for micro- and small enterprises within the meaning of Recommendation 2003/361/EC" [Art. 34(2)].
* **Maintaining compliance standards:** Despite adapting their processes, notified bodies must nevertheless "respect the degree of rigour and the level of protection required for the compliance of the high-risk AI system with the requirements of this Regulation" [Art. 34(2)].
answer_C:
Under the EU AI Act, notified bodies adapt their processes by taking into account specific characteristics of the provider and the AI system, while avoiding unnecessary burdens [Art. 31(8)], [Art. 34(2)]:

* **Company and system factors**: Notified bodies must have procedures and perform activities that take "due account of the size of a provider, the sector in which it operates, its structure, and the degree of complexity of the [high-risk] AI system concerned" [Art. 31(8)], [Art. 34(2)].
* **Minimising burdens for smaller entities**: When performing their activities, notified bodies must avoid unnecessary burdens for providers, "in particular in view of minimising administrative burdens and compliance costs for micro- and small enterprises within the meaning of Recommendation 2003/361/EC" [Art. 34(2)].
* **Maintained level of rigour**: Regardless of these adaptations, the notified body must "respect the degree of rigour and the level of protection required for the compliance of the high-risk AI system with the requirements of this Regulation" [Art. 34(2)].

question: How much time does a company have to fix or remove a non-compliant AI system if a regulator finds it poses a risk?
answer_A:
If a market surveillance authority evaluates an AI system presenting a risk and finds that it does not comply with the requirements and obligations of the Regulation, the relevant operator must take all appropriate corrective actions to bring the system into compliance, withdraw it from the market, or recall it:

* Within a period prescribed by the market surveillance authority, and 
* In any event "within the shorter of 15 working days, or as provided for in the relevant Union harmonisation legislation" [Art. 79(2)].

(Later amendments to the Act are not reflected in this text.)
answer_B:
If a market surveillance authority evaluates an AI system presenting a risk and finds that it does not comply with the requirements and obligations of the Regulation, the company (relevant operator) must take all appropriate corrective actions to bring the AI system into compliance, withdraw it from the market, or recall it:

* Within a period the market surveillance authority may prescribe [Art. 79(2)]; and 
* In any event, **within the shorter of 15 working days**, or as provided for in the relevant Union harmonisation legislation [Art. 79(2)].

*(Note: For dates of application or deadlines, later amendments to the Act are not reflected in this text.)*
answer_C: The market surveillance authority prescribes the specific period, but it must be **no longer than the shorter of 15 working days or the period provided for in the relevant Union harmonisation legislation** [Art. 79(2)]. This applies where the authority finds during its evaluation that the AI system presents a risk and does not comply with the Regulation, requiring corrective action, withdrawal, or recall [Art. 79(2)].

question: Do notified bodies have to share their assessment results with other similar bodies?
answer_B:
Yes. Under the EU AI Act, notified bodies are required to share assessment results and certificate information with other notified bodies as follows:

* **Conformity assessment results:** Each notified body must provide other notified bodies that carry out similar conformity assessment activities covering the same types of AI systems with "relevant information on issues relating to negative and, on request, positive conformity assessment results" [Art. 45(3)].
* **Quality management system approvals:** Notified bodies must inform other notified bodies of approvals they have "refused, suspended or withdrawn, and, upon request, of quality system approvals which it has issued" [Art. 45(2)(a)].
* **Union technical documentation assessment certificates:** Notified bodies must inform other notified bodies of certificates (or supplements) which they have "refused, withdrawn, suspended or otherwise restricted, and, upon request, of the certificates and/or supplements thereto which it has issued" [Art. 45(2)(b)].
answer_C: Yes. Each notified body must provide other notified bodies carrying out similar conformity assessment activities covering the same types of AI systems with relevant information on issues relating to negative conformity assessment results and, on request, positive conformity assessment results [Art. 45(3)].

question: Who oversees real-world testing of AI systems that are inside a regulatory sandbox?
answer_A:
Real-world testing of AI systems inside an AI regulatory sandbox is overseen and supervised by the following:

* **Market surveillance authorities**: They verify compliance with Article 60 as part of their supervisory role for the AI regulatory sandbox, and may allow testing in derogation from the conditions set out in Article 60(4), points (f) and (g) [Art. 76(2)].
* **National competent authorities / competent authorities**: The sandbox operates under their regulatory supervision pursuant to a sandbox plan [Art. 3(55)], [Art. 57(5)]. Where national competent authorities consider authorising real-world testing within a sandbox, they specifically agree on the terms, conditions, and appropriate safeguards with the participants to protect fundamental rights, health, and safety [Art. 58(4)].
* **Providers, prospective providers, and deployers**: Under the Article 60 conditions verified by market surveillance authorities [Art. 76(2)], the testing must be effectively overseen by the provider or prospective provider, as well as deployers or prospective deployers, through persons who are suitably qualified in the relevant field and have the necessary capacity, training, and authority [Art. 60(4)(j)].
answer_B: Real-world testing inside an AI regulatory sandbox is overseen by the **market surveillance authorities**, which verify compliance as part of their supervisory role for the sandbox [Art. 76(2)], and by the **national competent authority** that established the sandbox, which agrees the specific terms, conditions and safeguards for the testing [Art. 58(4)]. The sandbox is defined as a controlled framework set up by a competent authority under regulatory supervision [Art. 3(55)], and it may include testing in real world conditions supervised therein [Art. 57(5)].
answer_C:
Based on the provided excerpts, real-world testing of AI systems inside an AI regulatory sandbox is overseen and supervised by the following authorities and entities:

* **Market surveillance authorities:** Where testing in real world conditions is conducted for AI systems supervised within an AI regulatory sandbox under Article 58, market surveillance authorities verify compliance with Article 60 as part of their supervisory role for the sandbox [Art. 76(2)]. 
* **National competent authorities / Competent authorities:** AI regulatory sandboxes provide a controlled framework established by a competent authority under regulatory supervision [Art. 3(55)], [Art. 57(5)]. Where national competent authorities consider authorising real-world testing supervised within the sandbox framework, they specifically agree on the terms, conditions, and appropriate safeguards with participants to protect fundamental rights, health, and safety [Art. 58(4)].

question: Who can update the rules for general-purpose AI models when technology changes?
answer_A:
Under the EU AI Act, the **Commission** is empowered to update these rules through delegated acts in response to technological developments:

* **Classification thresholds, benchmarks, and indicators:** The Commission shall adopt delegated acts to amend the thresholds listed in Article 51(1) and (2) and supplement benchmarks and indicators "in light of evolving technological developments, such as algorithmic improvements or increased hardware efficiency, when necessary, for these thresholds to reflect the state of the art" [Art. 51(3)].
* **Criteria for systemic risk designation:** The Commission is empowered to adopt delegated acts to amend Annex XIII "by specifying and updating the criteria set out in that Annex" [Art. 52(4)].
* **Documentation and information requirements:** The Commission is empowered to adopt delegated acts "to amend Annexes XI and XII in light of evolving technological developments" [Art. 53(6)].
answer_B:
Under the EU AI Act, the **Commission** is empowered to update these rules by adopting delegated acts [Art. 51(3)], [Art. 52(4)], [Art. 53(6)]. 

Specifically, the Commission can:
* Amend the classification thresholds and supplement benchmarks and indicators "in light of evolving technological developments, such as algorithmic improvements or increased hardware efficiency, when necessary, for these thresholds to reflect the state of the art" [Art. 51(3)].
* Amend Annexes XI and XII (concerning technical documentation and information requirements for providers) "in light of evolving technological developments" [Art. 53(6)].
* Amend Annex XIII by specifying and updating the criteria used to designate a general-purpose AI model as presenting systemic risks [Art. 52(4)].

question: What sub-groups does the European AI Board have to create?
answer_A: The European Artificial Intelligence Board must establish **two standing sub-groups**: one for market surveillance authorities and one for notifying authorities, to provide a platform for cooperation on issues related to market surveillance and notified bodies respectively. The standing sub-group for market surveillance shall act as the administrative cooperation group (ADCO) for the Regulation [Art. 65(6)]. The Board may also establish other standing or temporary sub-groups as appropriate, but these are not mandatory [Art. 65(6)].
answer_B:
According to the AI Act, the Board is required to establish two standing sub-groups [Art. 65(6)]:

* A standing sub-group to provide a platform for cooperation and exchange among market surveillance authorities about issues related to market surveillance; this sub-group "should act as the administrative cooperation group (ADCO) for this Regulation within the meaning of Article 30 of Regulation (EU) 2019/1020" [Art. 65(6)].
* A standing sub-group to provide a platform for cooperation and exchange among notifying authorities about issues related to notified bodies [Art. 65(6)].

Additionally, while not mandatory, the Board "may establish other standing or temporary sub-groups as appropriate for the purpose of examining specific issues" [Art. 65(6)].
answer_C:
According to the AI Act, the European Artificial Intelligence Board must establish **two standing sub-groups** to provide a platform for cooperation and exchange [Art. 65(6)]:

* A standing sub-group for **market surveillance authorities** concerning issues related to market surveillance; this sub-group should act as the administrative cooperation group (ADCO) for the Regulation within the meaning of Article 30 of Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 [Art. 65(6)].
* A standing sub-group for **notifying authorities** concerning issues related to notified bodies [Art. 65(6)].

In addition, the Board is permitted (though not required) to establish other standing or temporary sub-groups as appropriate for examining specific issues [Art. 65(6)].

question: What does Article 31(6) require from notified bodies regarding fairness and independence?
answer_A: Article 31(6) requires notified bodies to be organised and operated so as to safeguard the "independence, objectivity and impartiality" of their activities, and to "document and implement a structure and procedures to safeguard impartiality and to promote and apply the principles of impartiality throughout their organisation, personnel and assessment activities" [Art. 31(6)].

* Be organized and operated in a manner that safeguards the "independence, objectivity and impartiality of their activities" [Art. 31(6)].
* Document and implement a structure and procedures designed to safeguard impartiality [Art. 31(6)].
* Promote and apply the principles of impartiality throughout their entire organization, personnel, and assessment activities [Art. 31(6)].
answer_C:
Under Article 31(6) of the EU Artificial Intelligence Act, notified bodies must satisfy the following requirements regarding independence, objectivity, and impartiality:

* They must be "organised and operated so as to safeguard the independence, objectivity and impartiality of their activities" [Art. 31(6)].
* They must "document and implement a structure and procedures to safeguard impartiality" [Art. 31(6)].
